title: Food & drink
goal: Name common foods and drinks, say what you like and want, describe tastes and order in a restaurant or at someone's home.
intro:
Sindhi food is rich, generous and often spicy: **Sindhi biryani** with potatoes and plums, **سائي ڀاڄي** (sāī bhāʄī, a green dish of spinach, dill and lentils), **ڪوڪي** (koki, a thick onion flatbread for breakfast) and the famous river fish **پلو** (palo). Meals are shared and guests are fed until they protest.

Grammatically, this unit introduces a key Sindhi pattern: the **'to me' (کي) construction**. Sindhi says 'to me water is needed' (مون کي پاڻي گهرجي) and 'to me biryani pleases' (مون کي برياني وڻي ٿي) instead of 'I want' and 'I like'.

vocab.note: f. ماني کائڻ = to eat (a meal). منجهند جي ماني = lunch, رات جي ماني = dinner.
f. سائي ڀاڄي = Sindhi 'green' dish of spinach and lentils.
f. پلو مڇي = palla/hilsa, the prized Indus fish.
m · pl انب anba. Sindh's mangoes (e.g. سنڌڙي sindhṛī) are famous.
f. Sindhi biryani is spicy, with potatoes and dried plums.
f. مون کي بک لڳي آهي = I'm hungry.
f. مون کي اڃ لڳي آهي = I'm thirsty.
Past: کاڌو khādho. Imperative: کائو khāo (polite), کاءُ khāu (intimate).
Past: پيتو pīto. Imperative: پيئو pīo (polite).
Used with کي: مون کي … گهرجي. Plural object: گهرجن ghurjan.
مون کي … وڻي ٿو/ٿي = I like …

phrases.native: مون کي هڪ ڪوپ چانهه گهرجي.
phrases.roman: moṃ khe hiku kopu chānhi ghurje.
phrases.en: I'd like a cup of tea.
What would you like to eat?

phrases.native: مون کي سائي ڀاڄي ڏاڍي وڻي ٿي.
phrases.roman: moṃ khe sāī bhāʄī ɗāḍhī vaṇe thī.

phrases.en: Please go easy on the chilli. (lit. keep chilli less)
That's enough, I'm full. (lit. the stomach got filled)

grammar.title: Wanting and needing: مون کي … گهرجي
grammar.body:
To say what you want or need, Sindhi puts the person in the **dative** with **کي** (khe, 'to') and uses **گهرجي** (ghurje, 'is needed'): **مون کي پاڻي گهرجي** — 'to me water is needed' = 'I want / need water'. The thing wanted is the grammatical subject, so گهرجي becomes **گهرجن** (ghurjan) if it is plural.

The oblique pronouns with کي are: مون کي (me), تو کي (you, intimate), هن کي (him/her), اسان کي (us), توهان کي (you, polite), هنن کي (them). In writing مون کي and تو کي are often run together: مونکي، توکي.

To **order or ask politely**, use the polite imperative ڏيو (ɗiyo) 'give': مون کي هڪ لسي ڏيو 'Give me a lassi'. You can also say مان … چاهيان ٿو 'I want …' (with a verb: کائڻ چاهيان ٿو 'I want to eat').

examples.native: اسان کي ٻه پليٽون برياني گهرجن.
examples.roman: asāṃ khe ɓa pleṭūṃ biryānī ghurjan.
examples.en: We'd like two plates of biryani.

grammar.title: Liking: مون کي … وڻي ٿو / ٿي
grammar.body:
'I like X' is expressed as **'X pleases me'**: مون کي + thing + **وڻي ٿو** (masculine thing) or **وڻي ٿي** (feminine thing); for plural things **وڻن ٿا / وڻن ٿيون**. Again the verb agrees with the thing liked, not with you.

مون کي چانهه وڻي ٿي — I like tea (چانهه f)
مون کي گوشت وڻي ٿو — I like meat (گوشت m)
مون کي انب وڻن ٿا — I like mangoes (m pl)

The negative uses **نٿو / نٿي** (na + tho, written as one word) before the verb: مون کي مڇي **نٿي** وڻي 'I don't like fish'. Add **ڏاڍو / ڏاڍي** 'very' for emphasis.

Notice also the hunger/thirst pattern with **لڳڻ** 'to strike, be felt': مون کي بک لڳي آهي 'hunger has struck me' = I'm hungry.

examples.native: هن کي انب ڏاڍا وڻن ٿا.
examples.roman: hun khe anba ɗāḍhā vaṇan thā.

examples.native: مون کي تکو کاڌو نٿو وڻي.
examples.roman: moṃ khe tikho khādho natho vaṇe.

dialogue.title: At a roadside restaurant
dialogue.setting: Ayaz and his friend Sarah stop at a dhaba on the highway near Hyderabad.

lines.speaker: Waiter
lines.native: ڀلي ڪري آيا، سائين! ڇا کائيندا؟
lines.roman: bhale kare āyā, sāīṃ! chhā khāīndā?
lines.en: Welcome, sir! What will you have?
lines.note: ڇا کائيندا؟ — a polite 'what will (you) eat?'

lines.speaker: Ayaz
lines.en: What is there? (lit. what-what is there)

lines.speaker: Waiter
lines.native: برياني، ڪڪڙ ڪڙاهي، دال، سائي ڀاڄي ۽ تازي مڇي.
lines.roman: biryānī, kukuṛu kaṛāhī, dāla, sāī bhāʄī ai tāzī machhī.
lines.en: Biryani, chicken karahi, dal, sai bhaji and fresh fish.

lines.speaker: Sarah
lines.native: مون کي سائي ڀاڄي ۽ ٻه مانيون گهرجن.
lines.roman: moṃ khe sāī bhāʄī ai ɓa mānyūṃ ghurjan.
lines.en: I'd like sai bhaji and two rotis.

lines.speaker: Ayaz
lines.native: ۽ مون کي برياني. مرچ گهٽ رکجو.
lines.roman: ai moṃ khe biryānī. marcha ghaṭu rakhijo.
lines.en: And biryani for me. Go easy on the chilli.

lines.speaker: Waiter
lines.native: پيئڻ لاءِ ڇا؟ لسي يا چانهه؟
lines.roman: pīaṇa lāi chhā? lasī yā chānhi?
lines.en: Anything to drink? Lassi or tea?

lines.speaker: Sarah
lines.native: ٿڌي لسي، مهرباني. مون کي اڃ لڳي آهي.
lines.roman: thadhī lasī, meharbānī. moṃ khe añu laɠī āhe.
lines.en: A cold lassi, please. I'm thirsty.

lines.speaker: Ayaz
lines.en: How is it? Do you like it?

lines.speaker: Sarah
lines.native: ڏاڍي سوادي آهي! پر ٿوري تکي آهي.
lines.roman: ɗāḍhī savādī āhe! para thorī tikhī āhe.
lines.en: It's delicious! But a bit spicy.

culture: Hospitality (مهمان نوازي) is a point of honour in Sindh. A guest is offered tea or a cold drink immediately, and refusing food once is expected politeness — your host will insist, and it is fine to accept the second time. Eating from shared dishes with the right hand and flatbread is normal at home. Sindhi Muslims eat halal meat and avoid pork and alcohol; many Hindu Sindhis are vegetarian or avoid beef. Famous Sindhi dishes to try: Sindhi biryani, sai bhaji with rice, koki for breakfast, and palo fish from the Indus, a seasonal delicacy around Hyderabad and Thatta.
